prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map separates the scene into a bright foreground coffee table within arm's reach (roughly 0.4–1.0 m directly in front of and below the camera wearer), a mid-ground grey armchair to the right (about 1.2–2.0 m away, angled toward the left), and a dark background media stand, floor, and windowsill (roughly 2.5–4.0 m ahead and to the left) with no other people present in the room. On the table, the smart display, white ribbed vase, and game board are brightest (roughly 0.4–0.6 m away), sitting just in front of the game controller, teal mug, silver vase, and small potted plant (0.6–0.9 m away, spaced 0.1–0.3 m apart from each other), while the display and vases partially occlude the mug, plant, and tabletop behind them. Across the five frames, the camera wearer turns slightly rightward in frame 5, shifting the armchair further into view on the right while the wearer's left hand enters at the bottom center (~0.4 m away) to touch the smart display and the right hand and remote rise at the bottom right (~0.3–0.4 m away). Compared to the RGB image, the depth map makes the continuous distance gradient across the transparent glass tabletop and the sharp depth boundary between the armchair and background wall much easier to read. However, the map is unreliable on the transparent glass tabletop (treating it as an opaque surface rather than seeing through to the floor below), loses detail in the very dark far-right background corner around the upright vacuum (~3.5–4.0 m away), and merges the wearer's fingers with the smart display surface in frame 5.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates discrete foreground and mid-ground objects against an unlabelled black background, identifying items on the coffee table within arm's reach (0.4–0.9 m in front of and below the camera wearer), the grey armchair to the right (1.2–2.0 m away, facing left), and high background objects (3.0–4.0 m away) with no people present. It captures the spatial layering and occlusions on the right side of the table—where the foreground white ribbed vase (~0.45 m away) partially occludes the teal mug (~0.6 m) to its upper left, and the silver vase (~0.7 m) sits in front of and partially occludes the potted plant (~0.85 m) further left—while showing their slight leftward shift in the frame as the camera turns slightly right in frame 5. The map highlights small, easily overlooked background objects in the RGB strip, such as the small potted plant high on the upper-right windowsill (~3.5 m away, frames 2–4) and the bottom edge of the wall-mounted TV on the upper left (~3.0 m away, frame 1), while cleanly separating overlapping tabletop items. However, it is highly unreliable in class consistency and completeness: it mislabels the foreground game board as a 'book' (frames 1 and 5), the white game controller as a 'cat' (frame 2), the smart display as a 'tv' (frames 3–4), and the white foreground vase as a 'cup', while alternating the armchair's label between 'couch' and 'chair'. It also completely misses the background media stand, the upright vacuum, the game board in frames 2–4, and the camera wearer's hands and remote at the bottom edge of the frame.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is completely black across all five frames, detecting neither body skeletons nor hand keypoints anywhere in the scene. Using the RGB strip for context, the room contains no other people facing or looking toward the camera wearer, leaving only static furniture and tabletop objects from 0.4 m to 4.0 m in front of the viewpoint. However, at the bottom edge of the frame within immediate arm's reach (~0.3–0.5 m below and in front of the camera wearer), the tip of a handheld remote is partly visible at the bottom-right corner in frames 1–4, and in frame 5 the camera wearer's left fingers reach onto the top edge of the smart display (~0.45 m away) while the right hand holds the remote at the bottom right (~0.35 m away) as the viewpoint turns slightly right. While the empty pose map accurately reflects the absence of other people in the room layout, it provides no spatial information that is hard to see in the RGB image. It is unreliable for egocentric hand tracking because it completely fails to detect the camera wearer's partially visible hands and fingers entering the lower field of view in the final frame.
